_comment: Preguntas ORIGINALES tipo NIE del capítulo 1.2 (Mens rea). No son preguntas reales del examen. Comprueba con tu edición 2027.

questions.scenario: PARKER sets fire to a house to claim insurance. He knows his neighbour's child is asleep inside and realises death is virtually certain, although he hopes the child will be rescued. The child dies. In relation to intention, which of the following is correct?
options: The jury may find that PARKER intended death if death was a virtual certainty and he appreciated that
PARKER cannot have intended death because he hoped the child would survive
The jury must find that PARKER intended death
Intention is irrelevant because murder only requires recklessness
explanations: Correct: R v Woollin (1998) – virtual certainty + appreciation allows the jury to find intention.
Incorrect: hoping for a different outcome does not prevent oblique intent.
Incorrect: the jury MAY find intention; it is not obliged to.
Incorrect: murder requires intention to kill or cause GBH.

questions.scenario: Under the Criminal Justice Act 1967, s. 8, when deciding whether a defendant intended or foresaw a result, a court or jury:
options: Must infer intention if the result was a natural and probable consequence
Must apply the standard of a reasonable person
Is not bound to infer intention just because the result was a natural and probable consequence, and must consider all the evidence
May only consider the defendant's own account
explanations: Incorrect: s. 8 says the opposite.
Incorrect: the test of intention is subjective.
Correct: the court decides by reference to all the evidence, drawing such inferences as appear proper.
Incorrect: all the evidence is considered.

questions.scenario: Two boys aged 11 and 12 set fire to newspapers behind a shop, expecting the fire to burn out. It spreads and causes £1 million damage. Neither boy foresaw any risk of the fire spreading. Which of the following is correct?
options: They were reckless because a reasonable adult would have foreseen the risk
They were not reckless because recklessness is subjective and they did not foresee the risk
They were reckless because criminal damage is a strict liability offence
They were reckless because of their age
explanations: Incorrect: the objective (Caldwell) test was abolished in R v G.
Correct: R v G (2003) – a person is reckless only if aware of the risk and it was unreasonable to take it.
Incorrect: criminal damage requires intention or recklessness.
Incorrect: age is relevant to what they actually foresaw, not a basis for liability.

questions.scenario: Which of the following best states the test for recklessness as to a result after R v G (2003)?
options: The defendant should have been aware of an obvious risk
The defendant intended the result
A reasonable person would have foreseen the result
The defendant was aware of a risk that the result would occur and, in the circumstances known to them, it was unreasonable to take the risk
explanations: Incorrect: 'should have been aware' is objective.
Incorrect: that is intention.
Incorrect: that is an objective test.
Correct: subjective awareness + unreasonable to take the risk.

questions.scenario: For the offence under s. 20 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 (malicious wounding/inflicting GBH), what must the defendant have foreseen?
options: That really serious harm would result
Nothing – s. 20 is strict liability
That some physical harm to some person, albeit of a minor character, might result
That death might result
explanations: Incorrect: foresight of serious harm is not required.
Incorrect: 'maliciously' requires intention or recklessness (Cunningham).
Correct: R v Savage; DPP v Parmenter (1991) – foresight of some harm is enough.
Incorrect: foresight of death is not required.

questions.scenario: What does the word 'maliciously' mean in statutory offences such as the Offences Against the Person Act 1861?
options: Intention or subjective recklessness
With ill will or spite
Negligently
Knowingly and dishonestly
explanations: Correct: R v Cunningham (1957).
Incorrect: it does not require spite or ill will.
Incorrect: negligence is objective.
Incorrect: these are different mental elements.

questions.scenario: A defendant is charged with theft and the jury must consider dishonesty. According to Ivey v Genting Casinos (2017), as applied in R v Barton and Booth (2020), what is the correct approach?
options: Ask whether the defendant thought what he did was dishonest
Ask only whether ordinary decent people would have done the same
Ask whether the defendant realised that ordinary decent people would consider it dishonest
Ascertain the defendant's actual state of knowledge or belief as to the facts, then decide whether the conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people
explanations: Incorrect: the defendant's own view of honesty is not the standard.
Incorrect: the defendant's knowledge or belief is considered first.
Incorrect: this was the second limb of Ghosh, which no longer applies.
Correct: the two-stage Ivey test.

questions.scenario: ADAMS throws a brick at COOK intending to hit him. COOK ducks and the brick hits and injures EVANS, who was standing behind. Which of the following is correct?
options: ADAMS cannot be liable for injuring EVANS because he did not intend to hit her
ADAMS's intention to injure COOK transfers to EVANS
ADAMS is liable only if he knew EVANS was there
ADAMS is liable only for an attempt against COOK
explanations: Incorrect: the doctrine of transferred mens rea applies.
Correct: R v Latimer (1886).
Incorrect: knowledge of the actual victim is not required.
Incorrect: he can also be liable for the offence against EVANS.

questions.scenario: FIELD throws a stone at a group of people intending to injure one of them. He misses and the stone breaks a shop window. Considering transferred mens rea, which of the following is correct?
options: His intent to injure does not transfer to criminal damage, although he might be reckless as to the window
His intent to injure transfers to the criminal damage
He cannot be liable for anything
He is liable for criminal damage because it is strict liability
explanations: Correct: R v Pembliton (1874) – but recklessness as to property damage may be proved separately.
Incorrect: mens rea only transfers between offences of the same kind.
Incorrect: an attempt to injure, or recklessness as to damage, may be available.
Incorrect: criminal damage requires intention or recklessness.

questions.scenario: FAGAN accidentally drives onto a police officer's foot. When told, he says 'wait' and switches off the engine. Which of the following is correct?
options: There is no offence because the act was accidental at the start
There is no offence because remaining stationary is an omission
The act was a continuing act and the mens rea formed during it can make it a battery
It is an offence only if he intended to drive onto the foot
explanations: Incorrect: the courts treated the act as continuing.
Incorrect: the court did not treat it as a mere omission.
Correct: Fagan v MPC (1969).
Incorrect: the mens rea can be formed during the continuing act.
questions.manualRef: Blackstone's 2027 · 1.2 · Coincidence of AR and MR

questions.scenario: A defendant attacks a victim intending to kill him. Believing the victim is dead, he throws the body off a cliff. In fact the victim was alive and dies from the fall. Which of the following is correct?
options: There is no murder because when he threw the body he did not intend to kill
The acts can be treated as one series of acts, so mens rea at the start is enough
He is only guilty of attempted murder
He is guilty of manslaughter only
explanations: Incorrect: the courts look at the whole transaction.
Correct: Thabo Meli v R (1954).
Incorrect: murder can be established.
Incorrect: murder is possible on these facts.

questions.scenario: What is meant by an offence of 'strict liability'?
options: An offence with no actus reus
An offence that can only be tried in the Crown Court
An offence requiring intention
An offence where no mens rea is required for at least one element of the actus reus
explanations: Incorrect: all offences have an actus reus.
Incorrect: mode of trial is unrelated.
Incorrect: the opposite.
Correct: mens rea is not needed for at least one element.

questions.scenario: When a statute creating a criminal offence is silent about mens rea, what is the starting point for the courts?
options: The offence is strict liability
Negligence is enough
There is a presumption that mens rea is required (Sweet v Parsley; B v DPP)
Intention must always be proved
explanations: Incorrect: strict liability is not presumed.
Incorrect: negligence is not presumed.
Correct: the presumption can be displaced only by clear words or necessary implication.
Incorrect: the required mental element depends on the offence.

questions.scenario: A person 'wilfully' neglects a child. According to R v Sheppard (1981), what does 'wilfully' mean?
options: Deliberately or recklessly
By accident
Negligently
With intention only
explanations: Correct: wilfully = deliberately or recklessly.
Incorrect: accidents are not wilful.
Incorrect: negligence is objective.
Incorrect: recklessness is also included.

questions.scenario: DEAN buys a laptop very cheaply from a man in a pub. He suspects it might be stolen but deliberately avoids asking any questions because he does not want to know. Considering 'knowledge', which of the following is correct?
options: Suspicion is always the same as knowledge
DEAN can never be said to know because he did not ask
Knowledge is irrelevant to handling stolen goods
Deliberately shutting one's eyes to the obvious can amount to knowledge
explanations: Incorrect: suspicion alone is not knowledge or belief.
Incorrect: deliberately avoiding the truth can amount to knowledge.
Incorrect: handling requires knowing or believing the goods are stolen.
Correct: 'wilful blindness' can amount to knowledge.

questions.scenario: Which of the following describes 'negligence' as a form of fault?
options: The defendant foresaw the risk and took it
The defendant's conduct fell below the standard expected of a reasonable person
The defendant intended the result
The defendant acted dishonestly
explanations: Incorrect: that is recklessness.
Correct: negligence is objective.
Incorrect: that is intention.
Incorrect: dishonesty is a separate concept.

questions.scenario: An offence of 'specific intent' is significant because:
options: Voluntary intoxication can be relevant to whether the defendant formed the intent
Voluntary intoxication is never relevant
It can be committed recklessly
It is always tried summarily
explanations: Correct: DPP v Majewski (1977) – for specific intent offences, voluntary intoxication may show the intent was not formed.
Incorrect: it can be relevant for specific intent offences.
Incorrect: specific intent offences require intention.
Incorrect: mode of trial is unrelated.

questions.scenario: Which of the following is an offence of basic intent, where voluntary intoxication is no defence?
options: Murder
Wounding with intent (s. 18 OAPA 1861)
Assault occasioning actual bodily harm (s. 47 OAPA 1861)
Theft
explanations: Incorrect: murder is specific intent.
Incorrect: s. 18 is specific intent.
Correct: s. 47 can be committed recklessly and is basic intent.
Incorrect: theft is generally treated as specific intent.

questions.scenario: MILLS fires a gun into a crowd 'to scare people', aware that someone might be hit. A person is killed. MILLS says he did not want anyone to die. Considering intention, which of the following is correct?
options: Desire is essential for intention
Foresight of a virtual certainty plus appreciation is evidence from which the jury may find intention
Foresight of death as a possibility automatically proves intention
Intention can never be found where the defendant did not want the result
explanations: Incorrect: oblique intent does not require desire.
Correct: Woollin – virtual certainty and appreciation; otherwise consider recklessness/manslaughter.
Incorrect: foresight of a mere possibility is not enough.
Incorrect: oblique intent is possible.

questions.scenario: In relation to direct intention, which of the following is correct?
options: The result must be likely to happen
The defendant must have planned the offence in advance
The defendant must have a motive
The result is the defendant's aim or purpose, however unlikely it is
explanations: Incorrect: likelihood is not required for direct intent.
Incorrect: premeditation is not required.
Incorrect: motive is different from intention.
Correct: direct intent = aim or purpose.

questions.scenario: Which statement about motive is correct?
options: A good motive is a defence
Motive is the same as intention
Motive is generally irrelevant to liability, although it may be relevant to evidence or sentence
Without a motive there can be no offence
explanations: Incorrect: a good motive does not prevent liability.
Incorrect: motive is why; intention is what the defendant aimed to do.
Correct.
Incorrect: motive is not an element.

questions.scenario: Under the Ivey test for dishonesty, how is the defendant's belief about the facts treated?
options: It is a matter of evidence; the reasonableness of the belief goes to whether it was genuinely held
It must be reasonable to count
It is irrelevant
Only beliefs supported by documents count
explanations: Correct.
Incorrect: the belief does not have to be reasonable, but reasonableness helps decide if it was genuine.
Incorrect: it is the first stage of the test.
Incorrect: there is no such rule.

questions.scenario: A 'state of mind' word 'believing' (e.g. in handling stolen goods) is best described as:
options: The same as suspecting
More than knowing
Only possible if the defendant was told
Less than knowing but more than mere suspicion
explanations: Incorrect: suspicion is not enough.
Incorrect: knowledge is the higher state.
Incorrect: belief can be inferred from circumstances.
Correct.

questions.scenario: Considering recklessness, which of the following matters when deciding whether it was 'unreasonable to take the risk'?
options: The circumstances as a reasonable person would have known them
The circumstances known to the defendant
Only the size of the risk
Whether the defendant had insurance
explanations: Incorrect: the test refers to circumstances known to the defendant.
Correct: R v G.
Incorrect: the social value of the conduct and other factors also matter.
Incorrect: irrelevant.

questions.scenario: HUGHES is very drunk and, in a fight, wounds a man with a broken glass. He is charged with wounding with intent (s. 18 OAPA 1861). His intoxication was voluntary. Which of the following is correct?
options: Evidence of intoxication may be considered on whether he formed the specific intent; if not, s. 20 may still apply
Intoxication is irrelevant to s. 18
He must be acquitted of everything
Voluntary intoxication is a complete defence to all offences
explanations: Correct: a drunken intent is still an intent, but if no intent was formed, s. 20 (basic intent) may apply.
Incorrect: s. 18 is a specific intent offence.
Incorrect: s. 20 remains available.
Incorrect: it is never a defence to basic intent offences.

questions.scenario: A licensee is charged with a regulatory offence that the court holds to be strict liability as to one element. Which of the following is correct?
options: The prosecution need not prove any mens rea for any element
The defendant must prove he was not negligent
The prosecution need not prove mens rea for that element, but may need to for others
Strict liability offences cannot be tried in court
explanations: Incorrect: strict liability may apply only to part of the offence.
Incorrect: unless a statutory defence places that burden, there is no general requirement.
Correct.
Incorrect: they are tried normally.

questions.scenario: Which of the following is correct about the relationship between actus reus and mens rea?
options: They must always occur at exactly the same second
They must coincide, but the courts may treat a continuing act or a series of acts as one transaction
Mens rea formed after the actus reus is always enough
Mens rea formed before the act is never enough
explanations: Incorrect: the courts are flexible.
Correct: Fagan; Thabo Meli; Church.
Incorrect: subsequent mens rea is not generally enough.
Incorrect: in a series of acts it may be.

questions.scenario: JAMES intends to kill his rival by shooting him, but aims badly and kills a stranger instead. With which offence can JAMES be charged in relation to the stranger?
options: Manslaughter only
No offence, because he did not know the stranger
Attempted murder only
Murder, because his intention to kill transfers
explanations: Incorrect: murder is available through transferred malice.
Incorrect: knowledge of the victim is not required.
Incorrect: the completed offence is murder.
Correct: transferred mens rea (same type of offence).

questions.scenario: A person 'intentionally' damages property. In R v G terms, what extra fault word, if added to the offence, would also allow conviction where the person did not intend the damage?
options: Maliciously only
Negligently
Recklessly
Knowingly
explanations: Incorrect: 'maliciously' is a word used in other statutes.
Incorrect: negligence is not enough for criminal damage.
Correct: criminal damage can be committed intentionally or recklessly.
Incorrect: knowledge is a different concept.

questions.scenario: Which of the following statements about the old 'Caldwell' objective recklessness is correct today?
options: It was overruled by R v G (2003); recklessness is now subjective
It still applies to criminal damage
It applies to all offences against the person
It applies only to children
explanations: Correct.
Incorrect: it no longer applies.
Incorrect: it never applied there and no longer applies anywhere in this context.
Incorrect: R v G removed it entirely.
